Job diary entry

I didn't get the first job that I applied to, but it's not the end of the world, is it? I have to keep positive. I should keep plugging away at it, shouldn't I? The organization system that I started will help a lot.
Also, I think that attending job fairs is a great way to add to a job search, don't you? So I've done some research and some thinking on how to make this job fair a useful and beneficial experience. Here are some tips which, if followed, will make attending job fairs worth your time.

Before you go, you should know about the employers that are attending. Do lots of groundwork about the companies so you have a sense of what the organization does and if there is a fit between your skills and interests. Make sure you have lots of copies of your résumé to give to the people who you have conversations with. Prepare a 20 to 30 second introduction to use with employers. You want to put your best foot forward, don't you?

Next, at the job fair, remember that the manners and mannerisms which you use are very important. Good handshakes are critical, aren't they? Remember to be friendly and conversational but resist treating the job fair as a social event. You want to focus your attention and energy on the people who may be future employers! After the fair, be sure you follow up with the recruiters you met. You can thank them for speaking with you and express interest in any opportunities that come up at the company.

Subject and Object Relative Clauses

When you want to clarify which person or thing you are talking about, you can use a relative clause.
You can use relative clauses to give more information about something without beginning a new sentence.
You can begin a relative clause with who for people, which for things or that for either people or things.
You can put the relative clause after the subject or the object of the sentence.
A subject relative clause describes the subject of the clause and follows the subject of the sentence.
An object relative clause describes the object of the clause and follows the object of the sentence.
A defining relative clause specifies which noun we are talking about:

• I didn't get the first job that I applied to.
  • (If you don't say 'that I applied to', the listener doesn't know which job you mean. This is necessary information).
A non-defining relative clause provides extra information about something. This information is not necessary to understand the sentence.

• Here are some tips which will make attending job fairs worth your time.
  • (Everybody knows what tips are, so 'which will make attending job fairs worth your time.' is extra information).

Tag Questions
You use tag questions to ask for clarification and confirmation.
Tag questions are short questions that are added at the end of statements.
They are used mostly in spoken English when you want to:

• confirm whether something is true or not, or
  • to encourage a response from someone you are speaking to.

1. An affirmative statement is followed by a negative tag question. Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying 'yes'.
    • You were at the job fair, weren't you?
    • You are going to the job fair, aren't you?
    • She has a résumé, doesn't she?
    • He can write a résumé, can't he?

1. A negative statement is followed by an affirmative tag question. Use this when you think the other person will agree by saying 'no'.
    • You weren't at the job fair, were you?
    • You aren't going to the job fair, are you?
    • She doesn't have a résumé, does she?
    • He can't write a résumé, can he?
If the main verb is to be or a modal verb, the tag will be the same.
For all other main verbs, use the tag do/does or did/didn't. Look at the examples in the chart.
